doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Short's hotel gig, forming the Carlyle band and the Street of Dreams arrangement
summary: A one-off hotel gig leads to a ten-week Carlyle run; his esoteric Street of Dreams arrangement flopped due to seating; other arrangers took over.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: jokingly, I said like, “Hey man” I said, “you know, you know what you need, you need a big band.” I said, like I did for, you know, like I said, joking, a big band with Bobby Short. Well I got a phone call from him about six months later saying, “You know you mentioned a band and you know, I can’t afford a big band.” I said, “I was just joking, Bobby, Jesus, you know.” He said, “Well I’ll tell you what, I have one gig” at some hotel, not the Carlyle but like a one night off gig, and I have some charts, and I’ve never really heard them, would you put — so I put together six horns, two trumpets, a trombone and three reeds. And we did this gig at some hotel here in Midtown, and the arrangements were really cheesy. They were really like what you would call like hotel band arrangements. Lot of whole notes and the harmonies were all just pudding or you know, vanilla, oatmeal, or whatever you call it. Nothing really there, but it sounded good. They were good arrangements. And that was that. And then he called back and said, “I’m going into the Carlyle in the fall and I think I’d like to try the band for ten weeks” you know, five nights a week, ten weeks, and I’d like to try it but I’m going to need some arrangements, because you know those arrangements I have are really pedestrian. So I started to arrange for the band. And pretty soon found that there were people who do it better than I could but that came a little bit later. So I put together a band. And the band was John Eckert and Virgil Jones, two trumpets, the trombone was split 50/50 between Eddie Bert and Bobby Pring, and the saxophones were myself, Scott Robinson and Jack Stooky or Jay Branford. And we joined Bobby’s trio, he had a bass and drum. And it went well although something funny happened. Bobby used to do a great version of “On the Street of Dreams.” And he asked me to write an arrangement. So I listened to his record, and this was part of why I eventually hired other arrangers. I didn’t realize it but I think subconsciously I was trying to educate him, but I was trying to write a sophisticated arrangement a little beyond what he was doing at the piano and, it was a big error, but I didn’t know it. So I wrote this esoteric arrangement. It wasn’t bad. But it wasn’t as good as the stuff that came later. So we did it. Now the funny thing was at the Carlyle the first season we were there I didn’t know it, the brass was here then there was Bobby and the piano, and over on the other side of the bass, on the other side of the room, were the three reeds. So I wrote an arrangement of “Street of Dreams” with the bass clarinet and trombone, muted trombone, playing some kind of esoteric counter line to Bobby in some kind of harmony. It sounded like, like you know if Anton Webern, you know, was sick, and incapacitated. It was horrible. Atonal, without the other note. So all the people sitting on one side of the room just heard [scats] it was horrible. Well they changed the configuration of the band and we eventually all sat together, and then Mark Lopeman and James Chirillo and Mike Christiansen started writing stuff.
